newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Raytheon Brazil project hits hiccup.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Raytheon Brazil project hits hiccup.

text.p: A $1.4 billion contract for an Amazonian radar surveillance system awarded by Brazil to U.S. high-technology and heavy engineering giant Raytheon Co has run into new hiccups.

Raytheon, which has seen the deal thrown to the wolves and then rescued again on several occasions over the past two years as the Brazilian Congress bickered over its cost, said it saw no reason to be concerned.

The latest obstacle to the project, known by its Portuguese acronym Sivam, came from the government's financial watchdog, the Federal Accounts Tribunal (TCU), which asked prosecutors to investigate before it judged a complaint brought by a senator.

Senator Antonio Carlos Valadares has alleged that Raytheon plans to set up only half the number of radar stations originally agreed for the surveillance system and that their unit costs had been considerably increased.
"The TCU decided it needed a deeper investigation before it could evaluate the case," TCU spokesman Marcos Santos said.

Apart from aiding air traffic control, Sivam will help Brazil detect epidemics, monitor environmental destruction, increase weather forecasting accuracy and combat drugs and contraband smuggling in the vastness of the Amazon river basin.

Raytheon's director of international public affairs, Barry French, said the company had not yet had the opportunity to fully evaluate the TCU move, but that first signs indicated there was "nothing unusual" about it.
"Our first reaction was essentially that there didn't seem to be any surprises that we should be concerned about," French told Reuters by telephone from Raytheon's Rio de Janeiro office.
French said the original plan foresaw a total of 24 radars. But the Brazilian government had since come up with four radars from its own inventory it would like to use for cost reasons.
French said the resulting savings would remain with the government and not with Raytheon or subcontractors. The project's value, for financing purposes, remains $1.4 billion.
Combining air and land-based radar with infrared satellite sensors, Sivam is dependent on financing by the U.S. Eximbank.
The Brazilian Senate finally approved the financing terms last May after months of haggling during which Sivam was frequently held hostage to other domestic concerns.
The Eximbank this week approved the credit, but physical work has yet to begun while Raytheon sorts out some financing details and "dots the i's and crosses the t's," French said.
French said he thought there had not been any undue delay in starting work on Sivam following the Senate go-ahead.
"I don't think it could have gone any faster," he said.
The Eximbank financing covers $1.022 billion. It will be supplemented by $85 million from the Swedish Development Bank, $239.2 million from Raytheon and $48 million from suppliers.
